Row 1: two glucose hexagons with an O bridge between C-1 of the first and C-4 of the second; label 'glycosidic bond' and write 'polysaccharide; formed by loss of H<sub>2</sub>O'. Row 2: two amino acids written H<sub>2</sub>N−CH(R<sub>1</sub>)−COOH and H<sub>2</sub>N−CH(R<sub>2</sub>)−COOH, an arrow with '−H<sub>2</sub>O', and the dipeptide H<sub>2</sub>N−CH(R<sub>1</sub>)−CO−NH−CH(R<sub>2</sub>)−COOH with the −CO−NH− boxed and labelled 'peptide bond'. Row 3: two pentose rings one above the other with a phosphate between them, one P−O bond to C-3' of the upper sugar and one to C-5' of the lower; label 'phosphodiester bond' and 'sugar-phosphate backbone of DNA/RNA'; put a base on C-1' of each sugar.

ncert_questions.a: Macromolecules (biomacromolecules) are large organic molecules of molecular weight 10,000 daltons or more, formed by the polymerisation of many small monomers joined by covalent bonds. They are found in the acid-insoluble fraction when a tissue is ground in trichloroacetic acid. Examples: proteins (polymers of amino acids, e.g. collagen, insulin, enzymes), polysaccharides (polymers of monosaccharides, e.g. starch, cellulose, glycogen), nucleic acids (polymers of nucleotides: DNA, RNA). Lipids are also found in the acid-insoluble fraction but are not true macromolecules, since their molecular weight is below 800 Da; they appear there because membrane lipids form insoluble vesicles on grinding.

ncert_questions.q: Illustrate a glycosidic, peptide and a phospho-diester bond.
ncert_questions.a:
Glycosidic bond: the bond between two monosaccharides in a polysaccharide, formed by dehydration between the −OH on C-1 of one sugar and the −OH on C-4 of the next, leaving an oxygen bridge C1−O−C4. Draw two glucose rings joined through the bridging oxygen and label it. Glucose + glucose → maltose + H2O is an example.

Peptide bond: the −CO−NH− bond between two amino acids in a polypeptide, formed by dehydration between the carboxyl group of one amino acid and the amino group of the next. Write H2N−CH(R1)−COOH + H2N−CH(R2)−COOH → H2N−CH(R1)−CO−NH−CH(R2)−COOH + H2O and box the −CO−NH−.

Phosphodiester bond: the bond between two nucleotides in DNA or RNA. One phosphate group is esterified to the C-3' hydroxyl of the sugar of one nucleotide and to the C-5' hydroxyl of the sugar of the next; since the phosphate forms two ester bonds it is a diester. Draw two pentose rings one below the other joined through a phosphate between C-3' of the upper and C-5' of the lower, with a base on C-1' of each, and label the sugar-phosphate backbone. All three are covalent bonds formed by loss of water.

ncert_questions.q: What is meant by tertiary structure of proteins?
ncert_questions.a: The tertiary structure of a protein is the three-dimensional shape produced when the long polypeptide chain, already coiled into helices and sheets in parts (secondary structure), folds upon itself like a hollow woollen ball. It gives a three-dimensional view of the protein, with the folds held by hydrogen bonds, ionic bonds, disulphide bridges and hydrophobic interactions between R groups. The tertiary structure is absolutely necessary for the biological activity of proteins: for example, the folding creates the crevices or pockets that serve as the active sites of enzymes. Loss of tertiary structure (denaturation by heat or extreme pH) destroys the activity.

ncert_questions.q: Proteins have primary structure. If you are given a method to know which amino acid is at either of the two termini (ends) of a protein, can you connect this information to purity or homogeneity of a protein?
ncert_questions.a: Yes. The primary structure of a protein is its sequence of amino acids, with one free amino group at the N-terminal end and one free carboxyl group at the C-terminal end; each polypeptide chain therefore has exactly one N-terminal and one C-terminal amino acid. If a protein sample is pure and homogeneous (all molecules identical), end-group analysis will detect only one kind of N-terminal amino acid and one kind of C-terminal amino acid. If the sample is a mixture of different proteins, more than one N-terminal or C-terminal amino acid will be found. Thus terminal amino acid analysis can be used as a test of purity. (For a protein with several identical subunits, such as haemoglobin's α and β chains, the number of different terminal residues also indicates how many kinds of chain are present.)

A triglyceride is a lipid made of one molecule of glycerol and three molecules of fatty acids. Glycerol is trihydroxy propane, a three-carbon compound with three hydroxyl (−OH) groups. Each −OH group is esterified with the carboxyl group (−COOH) of a fatty acid with loss of one molecule of water, so a triglyceride contains three ester bonds and its formation releases three molecules of water. The fatty acids may be the same or different, and may be saturated (no C=C double bonds, e.g. palmitic acid, 16 carbons) or unsaturated (one or more C=C, e.g. oleic acid). Triglycerides with mainly saturated fatty acids are solid fats; those with unsaturated fatty acids have lower melting points and are oils (e.g. gingely oil). Triglycerides are the storage form of energy in adipose tissue and seeds. Glycerol + 3 fatty acids → triglyceride + 3H2O.

ncert_questions.q: Can you describe what happens when milk is converted into curd or yoghurt, from your understanding of proteins?
ncert_questions.a: Milk contains the globular protein casein in the form of a colloidal suspension. When milk is inoculated with lactic acid bacteria (Lactobacillus), the bacteria ferment the milk sugar lactose to lactic acid. The acid lowers the pH of the milk. At this lower pH the ionic and hydrogen bonds that hold the tertiary structure of casein are disrupted, the protein is denatured and its molecules unfold and aggregate; the globular protein changes into an insoluble, fibrous, coagulated mass. This coagulation of casein is what we see as the thickening of milk into curd or yoghurt. The change is a change in the higher-order structure of the protein (secondary and tertiary), not in its primary structure; the amino acid sequence remains the same, which is why the nutritional value of the protein is unchanged.

ncert_questions.q: Draw the structure of the amino acid, alanine.
ncert_questions.a: Alanine is an α-amino acid in which the R group is a methyl group (−CH3). Draw the α-carbon in the centre with four substituents: a hydrogen atom (H) above, an amino group (H2N−) on the left, a carboxyl group (−COOH) on the right and the methyl group (CH3) below. In one line: CH3−CH(NH2)−COOH. Label the α-carbon and the three functional parts (amino group, carboxyl group, R group). In the zwitterionic form the groups are written H3N+− and −COO−.

ncert_questions.q: What are gums made of? Is Fevicol different?
ncert_questions.a: Gums are secondary metabolites of plants (NCERT Table 9.3 lists them under polymeric substances). Chemically they are heteropolysaccharides: long chains of several different monosaccharide units and their derivatives, such as arabinose, galactose, glucuronic acid and rhamnose, joined by glycosidic bonds. They are hydrophilic, swell in water and are exuded by plants such as Acacia (gum arabic) to seal wounds. Fevicol is different. It is a synthetic adhesive based on a man-made polymer (polyvinyl acetate in an emulsion), not a polysaccharide and not a product of any living organism; it cannot be digested and does not swell in water like a natural gum.

ncert_questions.q: Find out a qualitative test for proteins, fats and oils, amino acids and test any fruit juice, saliva, sweat and urine for them.
ncert_questions.a: Proteins: Biuret test. Add a few drops of dilute NaOH and then 1 per cent CuSO4 solution to the sample; a violet or purple colour shows peptide bonds, i.e. protein. Fats and oils: grease-spot test (or Sudan III test). Rub or drop the sample on paper; a translucent, permanent greasy spot shows fat or oil. With Sudan III the fat stains red. Amino acids: ninhydrin test. Heat the sample with ninhydrin solution; a purple-blue colour shows free amino acids. (Starch is tested with iodine, blue-black; reducing sugars with Benedict's solution, brick red.) Typical results: fruit juice gives a positive Benedict's test (sugars) and a weak ninhydrin test (free amino acids), no Biuret and no grease spot. Saliva gives a positive Biuret test (the enzyme amylase and mucin are proteins). Sweat gives a faint ninhydrin test (traces of amino acids and urea) and is negative for protein and fat. Normal urine is negative for protein, fat and sugar; protein in urine is a sign of kidney disease.

ncert_questions.q: Describe the important properties of enzymes.
ncert_questions.a:
1. Chemical nature: almost all enzymes are proteins with a specific tertiary structure; some RNA molecules (ribozymes) also act as enzymes.

2. Active site: folding of the polypeptide creates crevices or pockets, the active sites, where the substrate binds and is converted to product.

3. Catalytic power: enzymes increase the rate of reactions enormously by lowering the activation energy; carbonic anhydrase speeds the hydration of CO2 from about 200 molecules per hour to about 600,000 per second, roughly 10 million times.

4. Not consumed: the enzyme is released unchanged at the end of the catalytic cycle (E + S → ES → EP → E + P) and is reused, so only tiny amounts are needed.

5. Specificity: each enzyme acts on a particular substrate or bond because of the precise shape and chemistry of its active site.

6. Thermolability: enzymes work best at an optimum temperature (about 37 °C for human enzymes), are temporarily inactivated by low temperature and destroyed (denatured) above about 40 °C; enzymes of thermophilic organisms remain active at 80 to 90 °C.

7. pH sensitivity: each enzyme has an optimum pH (pepsin about 2, trypsin about 8) on either side of which activity falls.

8. Dependence on substrate concentration: velocity rises with substrate concentration until a maximum velocity Vmax is reached when all enzyme molecules are occupied.

9. Inhibition: specific chemicals inhibit enzymes; a competitive inhibitor resembles the substrate and competes for the active site (malonate on succinic dehydrogenase).

10. Co-factors: many enzymes need non-protein co-factors (prosthetic groups such as haem, co-enzymes such as NAD, metal ions such as Zn2+) to be active; the protein part alone (apoenzyme) is inactive.

ncert_questions.q: Match the following: (a) ester bond, (b) glycosidic bond, (c) peptide bond, (d) hydrogen bond with (i) polysaccharide, (ii) protein, (iii) fat, (iv) water.
ncert_questions.a: (a) Ester bond → (iii) fat: the carboxyl group of a fatty acid is esterified with a hydroxyl group of glycerol. (b) Glycosidic bond → (i) polysaccharide: monosaccharides are linked through an oxygen bridge. (c) Peptide bond → (ii) protein: amino acids are joined by −CO−NH− links. (d) Hydrogen bond → (iv) water: the partially positive hydrogen of one water molecule is attracted to the oxygen of another. (Hydrogen bonds also hold the two DNA strands and the α-helix together, but they are not the bonds between monomers.)

ncert_questions.q: Match the following polysaccharides with where they are found: starch, cellulose, glycogen, chitin; cotton fibre, exoskeleton of cockroach, liver, peeled potato.
ncert_questions.a: Starch → peeled potato (the storage polysaccharide of plants; the cut surface turns blue-black with iodine). Cellulose → cotton fibre (cotton is nearly pure cellulose, the plant cell-wall polysaccharide). Glycogen → liver (the storage polysaccharide of animals, stored in liver and muscle). Chitin → exoskeleton of cockroach (the complex polysaccharide of N-acetyl glucosamine units in arthropod exoskeletons).

ncert_questions.q: Nucleic acids exhibit secondary structure. Justify with an example. Describe the secondary structure of DNA as given by Watson and Crick.
ncert_questions.a:
A secondary structure is a regular, repeating three-dimensional arrangement of a polymer chain held by hydrogen bonds. Nucleic acids show it: DNA exists as a double helix of two strands held by base-pair hydrogen bonds, and single-stranded RNA folds back on itself to form hairpins and the clover-leaf of tRNA. The best-known example is the Watson-Crick model of B-DNA, with the following salient features:

  1. DNA is made of two polynucleotide strands, each with a backbone of alternating sugar (2'-deoxyribose) and phosphate joined by phosphodiester bonds.
  2. The two strands are antiparallel: one runs 5'→3' and the other 3'→5'.
  3. The sugar-phosphate backbone is on the outside and the nitrogen bases project inside, perpendicular to the helix axis.
  4. The bases of the two strands are paired by hydrogen bonds: adenine with thymine by two hydrogen bonds and guanine with cytosine by three. So a purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, the two strands are complementary and the width of the helix is uniform.
  5. The two strands are coiled around a common axis into a right-handed double helix.
  6. The helix has a pitch of 34 Å (3.4 nm) with 10 base pairs per turn; the distance between adjacent base pairs, the rise, is 3.4 Å (0.34 nm).
  7. The stacking of the base pairs, together with the hydrogen bonds, gives the helix stability. Other forms of DNA (A, C, Z) also exist.

Draw the labelled double helix (see the diagrams section) to complete the answer.

ncert_questions.q: Formation of enzyme-substrate complex (ES) is the first step in catalysed reactions. Describe the other steps till the formation of product.
ncert_questions.a:
Every enzyme has a substrate-binding site, the active site, which is a pocket formed by the folding of the polypeptide. The overall course of the reaction is E + S → ES → EP → E + P, and the catalytic cycle proceeds in these steps:

  1. The substrate binds to the active site of the enzyme, fitting into it, and the highly reactive, short-lived enzyme-substrate complex (ES) is formed.
  2. The binding of the substrate induces the enzyme to alter its shape, so that it fits more tightly around the substrate (induced fit).
  3. The active site of the enzyme, now in close proximity to the substrate, breaks the chemical bonds of the substrate (or forms new ones); the substrate is converted to product while still bound, and the enzyme-product complex (EP) is formed.
  4. The enzyme releases the products, and the free enzyme, chemically unchanged, is ready to bind another molecule of substrate and run through the cycle again.

Because the substrate is held at the active site in a strained, reactive orientation, the energy needed to reach the transition state (the activation energy) is lowered, which is why the enzyme-catalysed reaction is so much faster than the uncatalysed one. Draw the four-stage cycle diagram with the active site labelled.

ncert_questions.q: What are enzyme classes? Explain any two with the type of reaction they catalyse.
ncert_questions.a:
Enzymes are classified into six classes on the basis of the type of reaction they catalyse, each class with 4 to 13 subclasses, and every enzyme is given a four-digit number. The six classes are oxidoreductases (dehydrogenases), transferases, hydrolases, lyases, isomerases and ligases. Two explained:

Hydrolases catalyse the hydrolysis (breaking by addition of water) of ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C−C, C−halide or P−N bonds. Example: trypsin hydrolyses peptide bonds of proteins; amylase hydrolyses glycosidic bonds of starch; lipase hydrolyses ester bonds of fats.

Ligases catalyse the linking together of two compounds, for instance the formation of C−O, C−S, C−N or P−O bonds, usually using energy from ATP. Example: DNA ligase joins two DNA fragments by forming a phosphodiester (P−O) bond; aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase joins an amino acid to its tRNA.

(Alternative pair: oxidoreductases catalyse S reduced + S' oxidised → S oxidised + S' reduced, e.g. succinic dehydrogenase; lyases remove groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving a double bond, X−C−C−Y → X−Y + C=C, e.g. decarboxylases.)

pyq.q: It is said that the elemental composition of living organisms and that of inanimate objects (like the earth's crust) are similar in the sense that all the major elements are present in both. What then is the difference between the two groups?
options: Living organisms have more gold in them than inanimate objects
Living organisms have more water in their body than inanimate objects
Living organisms have more carbon, oxygen and hydrogen per unit mass than inanimate objects
Living organisms have more calcium in them than inanimate objects
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Table 9.2 shows carbon at 18.5 per cent of body weight against 0.03 per cent in the crust, and oxygen and hydrogen also higher, because living matter is built of organic compounds. Calcium and sodium are actually higher in the crust.

pyq.q: Many elements are found in living organisms either free or in the form of compounds. Which one of the following is not found in living organisms?
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Silicon is 27.7 per cent of the earth's crust but negligible in the human body (Table 9.2); magnesium, iron and sodium are all present in living organisms.

pyq.q: An amino acid in solution at a particular pH carries a positively charged amino group and a negatively charged carboxyl group at the same time. This form is called the
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: The zwitterion has −NH<sub>3</sub><sup>+</sup> and −COO<sup>−</sup> on the same molecule; the net charge is zero but the molecule is not uncharged.

pyq.q: A nucleoside is formed when a nitrogen base is attached to a sugar. When a phosphate group is further attached, the compound formed is a
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: Base + sugar = nucleoside; nucleoside + phosphate = nucleotide (e.g. adenosine → adenylic acid). A nucleic acid is a polymer of many nucleotides.

pyq.q: Which of the following is a heteropolymer?
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Proteins contain up to 20 different amino acids, so they are heteropolymers. Cellulose and starch are homopolymers of glucose and inulin is a homopolymer of fructose.

pyq.q: The acid-soluble pool obtained on grinding a tissue in trichloroacetic acid roughly represents the composition of the
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: NCERT states that the acid-soluble pool represents roughly the cytoplasmic composition, while the macromolecules come from the cytoplasm and organelles together.

pyq.q: Carbonic anhydrase catalyses the reaction CO<sub>2</sub> + H<sub>2</sub>O → H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>. In the presence of the enzyme the number of H<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> molecules formed is about
pyq.answer: c
pyq.solution: Without the enzyme about 200 molecules form per hour; with carbonic anhydrase about 600,000 molecules form per second, an acceleration of about ten million times.

pyq.q: Malonate inhibits the activity of succinic dehydrogenase because malonate
options: closely resembles the substrate succinate and competes for the active site
binds to the co-factor of the enzyme
raises the activation energy of the reaction
pyq.answer: b
pyq.solution: This is NCERT's example of competitive inhibition: the inhibitor resembles the substrate in molecular structure and competes with it for the substrate-binding site.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Lipids are found in the acid-insoluble fraction of a ground tissue although they are not macromolecules. Reason (R): Lipids in the cell are arranged in membranes, which on grinding form vesicles that are not water-soluble.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Lipids have molecular weights below 800 Da, but membrane fragments form insoluble vesicles that are retained with the macromolecules; R explains A exactly as NCERT does.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): Starch gives a blue colour with iodine but cellulose does not. Reason (R): Starch forms helical secondary structures that can hold iodine molecules, whereas cellulose contains no complex helices.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: The starch-iodine complex forms because I<sub>2</sub> fits inside the starch helix; cellulose is a straight chain without helices, so no complex and no colour.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): All enzymes are proteins. Reason (R): Ribozymes are nucleic acids that behave like enzymes.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: d
pyq.solution: Almost all, not all, enzymes are proteins; the existence of ribozymes (catalytic RNA) makes A false and R true.

pyq.q: Assertion (A): The velocity of an enzyme-catalysed reaction does not rise beyond V<sub>max</sub> however much the substrate concentration is increased. Reason (R): At V<sub>max</sub> there are no free enzyme molecules left to bind with the additional substrate.
options: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
pyq.answer: a
pyq.solution: Once every active site is occupied the enzyme is saturated and the rate plateaus at the maximum velocity; R is exactly NCERT's reason.

pyq.q: Distinguish between a nucleoside and a nucleotide with one example of each.
pyq.answer: A nucleoside is a nitrogen base attached to a pentose sugar (ribose or 2'-deoxyribose) at C-1'; it has two components and no phosphate. Example: adenosine (adenine + ribose), cytidine, uridine. A nucleotide is a nucleoside with a phosphate group attached to C-5' of the sugar; it has three components, base + sugar + phosphate, and is the monomer of nucleic acids. Example: adenylic acid (AMP), guanylic acid, thymidylic acid.

pyq.q: What are primary and secondary metabolites? Give two examples of each.
pyq.answer: Primary metabolites are organic compounds that have identifiable functions in the physiological processes of the organism and are found in all cells: amino acids, sugars, fatty acids, nucleotides. Secondary metabolites are compounds found in plant, fungal and microbial cells that are not directly involved in normal growth and physiology and whose functions are often unknown, though many are useful to humans: alkaloids (morphine, codeine), pigments (carotenoids, anthocyanins), toxins (abrin, ricin), drugs (vinblastin, curcumin), rubber and gums.

pyq.q: Define activation energy. How do enzymes affect it?
pyq.answer: For a substrate S to be converted to product P it must first pass through a higher-energy, unstable transition state. The difference between the average energy content of the substrate and the energy of the transition state is the activation energy. Enzymes bind the substrate at the active site and strain its bonds, providing a path with a transition state of lower energy; they thus lower the activation energy, so that far more substrate molecules can cross the barrier per unit time and the rate rises enormously. Enzymes do not change the energy of S or P, nor the equilibrium of the reaction.

pyq.q: What is a co-factor? Name the three kinds of co-factors.
pyq.answer: A co-factor is a non-protein constituent that is bound to an enzyme and is needed to make the enzyme catalytically active; the protein part alone, the apoenzyme, is inactive, and apoenzyme plus co-factor is the holoenzyme. The three kinds are: (i) prosthetic groups, organic and tightly bound (haem in catalase); (ii) co-enzymes, organic and transiently bound during catalysis, often containing vitamins (NAD and NADP contain niacin); (iii) metal ions (zinc in carboxypeptidase).

pyq.q: Why is the melting point of an oil lower than that of a fat? Name a phospholipid found in the cell membrane.
pyq.answer: Fats and oils are both triglycerides, but oils contain a higher proportion of unsaturated fatty acids (with C=C double bonds), whose kinked chains cannot pack closely, so the intermolecular forces are weaker and the melting point is lower; oils are therefore liquid at room temperature (gingely oil) while fats, rich in saturated fatty acids, are solid. Lecithin is the phospholipid NCERT names as a component of the cell membrane.

pyq.q: Describe how you would analyse the chemical composition of a living tissue to find its organic and inorganic constituents.
pyq.answer:
Organic constituents. Take the living tissue (a vegetable or a piece of liver), grind it in trichloroacetic acid (Cl3CCOOH) with a mortar and pestle and strain the slurry through cheesecloth. The filtrate is the acid-soluble pool: it contains thousands of small organic compounds (amino acids, sugars, nucleotides, fatty acids, etc.) with molecular weights 18 to about 800 Da, and roughly represents the cytoplasm. The retentate is the acid-insoluble fraction, containing the macromolecules proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides (≥ 10,000 Da) and lipids (as membrane vesicles). Both fractions can be further analysed by chemical methods to identify each compound. (2 marks)

Inorganic constituents. Weigh a sample, dry it (loss = water) and then burn it completely so that all carbon compounds are oxidised to CO2 and water vapour. The residue, the ash, contains the inorganic elements (calcium, magnesium, etc.) and inorganic compounds (sulphate, phosphate), which can be identified by elemental analysis. (1 mark)

pyq.q: Give three differences between DNA and RNA on the basis of their chemical composition and structure.
pyq.answer:
• Sugar: DNA contains 2'-deoxyribose; RNA contains ribose (with an −OH at C-2').
  • Nitrogen bases: DNA has adenine, guanine, cytosine and thymine; RNA has adenine, guanine, cytosine and uracil in place of thymine.
  • Strands: DNA is usually double-stranded, the two antiparallel strands forming a right-handed double helix held by A=T and G≡C hydrogen bonds (Watson-Crick model); RNA is usually single-stranded, though it may fold back on itself to form secondary structures (hairpins, clover-leaf of tRNA).

Additional points if asked: DNA is the genetic material in most organisms and is chemically more stable, whereas RNA is mostly involved in protein synthesis (mRNA, tRNA, rRNA) and is less stable; some RNAs (ribozymes) act as enzymes. One mark per difference.

pyq.q: Explain the four levels of protein structure with one example.
pyq.answer: Primary structure: the linear sequence of amino acids in the polypeptide, joined by peptide bonds, from the N-terminal amino acid (free −NH2) to the C-terminal amino acid (free −COOH). It determines all the higher levels. Secondary structure: regular local folding of the chain held by hydrogen bonds between backbone groups; the thread is coiled into a right-handed α-helix (only right-handed helices occur in proteins) or laid side by side as a β-pleated sheet. Tertiary structure: the whole chain, with its helices and sheets, folded upon itself like a hollow woollen ball to give a compact three-dimensional shape; it is absolutely necessary for biological activity, e.g. it creates the active site of an enzyme. Quaternary structure: in proteins made of more than one polypeptide, the arrangement of the folded subunits with respect to one another; adult human haemoglobin has four subunits, two α and two β. Draw the four-panel diagram to support the answer.

pyq.q: What is competitive inhibition? Explain with an example and state one use of competitive inhibitors.
pyq.answer:
Enzyme activity is sensitive to specific chemicals that bind to the enzyme; when such binding shuts off the activity, the process is inhibition and the chemical is an inhibitor. In competitive inhibition the inhibitor closely resembles the substrate in molecular structure and therefore competes with the substrate for the active site. While the inhibitor occupies the site the substrate cannot bind, so the rate of the reaction falls; because the two compete, the inhibition can be reduced by increasing the substrate concentration. (1½ marks)

Example: malonate closely resembles the substrate succinate and inhibits succinic dehydrogenase, the enzyme of the Krebs cycle that oxidises succinate to fumarate. (1 mark)

Use: competitive inhibitors are used in the control of bacterial pathogens: a drug that mimics a bacterial substrate blocks the bacterial enzyme (sulpha drugs resemble para-aminobenzoic acid and block folic acid synthesis in bacteria). (½ mark)

pyq.q: Name the three kinds of co-factors and explain each with one example. What happens to enzyme activity when the co-factor is removed?
pyq.answer: Co-factors are non-protein constituents bound to the apoenzyme (protein part) to form the active holoenzyme. (i) Prosthetic groups: organic compounds tightly bound to the apoenzyme; in peroxidase and catalase, which break hydrogen peroxide into water and oxygen (2H2O2 → 2H2O + O2), haem is the prosthetic group and forms part of the active site. (ii) Co-enzymes: organic compounds whose association with the apoenzyme is transient, usually only during catalysis; they serve many different enzymes, and many contain vitamins, e.g. NAD and NADP contain niacin. (iii) Metal ions: a number of enzymes require metal ions that form coordination bonds with side chains at the active site and with the substrate; zinc is the co-factor of the proteolytic enzyme carboxypeptidase. When the co-factor is removed the catalytic activity is lost, which shows that co-factors play a crucial role in enzyme activity.

pyq.q: Explain the effect of (a) temperature, (b) pH, (c) substrate concentration and (d) inhibitors on the activity of an enzyme. Draw suitable graphs.
pyq.answer:
Enzyme activity depends on conditions that affect the tertiary structure of the protein and the active site.

(a) Temperature. Each enzyme shows its highest activity at an optimum temperature (about 37 °C for human enzymes) and activity falls on either side, giving a bell-shaped curve. At low temperature the enzyme is preserved in a temporarily inactive state and recovers on warming. At high temperature (above about 40 °C) the protein is denatured, the active site is destroyed and activity is lost permanently. Enzymes of thermophilic organisms remain active up to 80 to 90 °C. (1½ marks with graph)

(b) pH. Each enzyme has an optimum pH at which activity is maximum (pepsin about 2, trypsin about 8); a change of pH on either side alters the ionisation of the amino acids of the active site and the substrate, and at extreme pH the enzyme is denatured. The curve is again bell-shaped. (1 mark with graph)

(c) Substrate concentration. With increasing substrate concentration the velocity of the reaction rises at first, then rises more slowly and finally reaches a maximum velocity Vmax, which is not exceeded by any further rise in substrate concentration, because there are no free enzyme molecules left to bind the additional substrate; all active sites are occupied. The graph is a curve rising from the origin and flattening into a plateau at Vmax. (1½ marks with graph)

(d) Inhibitors. Specific chemicals that bind to the enzyme and shut off its activity are inhibitors. A competitive inhibitor closely resembles the substrate and competes for the active site, e.g. malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase because it resembles succinate; the inhibition can be overcome by more substrate. Such inhibitors are used to control bacterial pathogens. (1 mark)

pyq.q: What is a metabolic pathway? Explain the concept of activation energy with an energy diagram and describe how an enzyme brings about a high rate of reaction.
pyq.answer:
Metabolic pathway. Most reactions in a cell are multistep: a substrate is converted to the final product through a series of intermediate reactions, each catalysed by its own enzyme. Such a series is a metabolic pathway; the reactants, intermediates and products are metabolites. Example: in glycolysis glucose is converted to pyruvic acid in ten steps, each with a different enzyme. The same glucose ends as pyruvic acid aerobically, lactic acid in anaerobic muscle and ethanol in fermenting yeast. (1 mark)

Activation energy. For a substrate S to become the product P, S must pass through a higher-energy, unstable transition state. The difference between the average energy of S and the energy of the transition state is the activation energy. In the energy diagram (energy on the y-axis, progress of reaction on the x-axis) the curve rises from the level of S to a peak, the transition state, and falls to the level of P. If P lies below S the reaction is exothermic and spontaneous; if P lies above S it is endothermic; in both cases the peak must be crossed, and the height of the peak decides how fast the reaction goes. (2 marks with diagram)

How enzymes raise the rate. The enzyme binds the substrate at its active site to form the enzyme-substrate complex; the binding holds the substrate in a strained, reactive orientation, so the reaction proceeds through a transition state of lower energy. The enzyme thus lowers the activation energy (draw a second, lower peak labelled 'with enzyme'), so that at the same temperature many more substrate molecules have enough energy to cross the barrier per unit time and the rate is enormously increased. The enzyme is released unchanged (E + S → ES → EP → E + P) and is used again. Example: carbonic anhydrase raises the hydration of CO2 from about 200 molecules per hour to about 600,000 per second, roughly ten million times. Enzymes do not alter the energy of S or P or the equilibrium; they only speed the approach to it. (2 marks)

pyq.q: Describe the classification and nomenclature of enzymes. Give the type of reaction catalysed by each class with one example.
pyq.answer:
Thousands of enzymes have been isolated and studied, and they are classified into six classes on the basis of the type of reaction they catalyse. Each class has 4 to 13 subclasses, and every enzyme is named with a four-digit number (class, subclass, sub-subclass, serial number). (1 mark)

  1. Oxidoreductases (dehydrogenases): catalyse oxidoreduction between two substrates, S reduced + S' oxidised → S oxidised + S' reduced. Example: succinic dehydrogenase, alcohol dehydrogenase.
  2. Transferases: catalyse the transfer of a group G (other than hydrogen) between a pair of substrates, S−G + S' → S + S'−G. Example: transaminases (amino group), hexokinase (phosphate group).
  3. Hydrolases: catalyse hydrolysis of ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C−C, C−halide or P−N bonds. Example: amylase, lipase, trypsin.
  4. Lyases: catalyse removal of groups from substrates by mechanisms other than hydrolysis, leaving double bonds, X−C−C−Y → X−Y + C=C. Example: decarboxylases, aldolase.
  5. Isomerases: catalyse inter-conversion of optical, geometric or positional isomers. Example: phosphohexose isomerase (glucose-6-phosphate ⇌ fructose-6-phosphate).
  6. Ligases: catalyse the linking together of two compounds, forming C−O, C−S, C−N or P−O bonds, usually with ATP. Example: DNA ligase, aminoacyl-tRNA synthetase.

(4 marks, two-thirds of a mark per class with its reaction type and example)

pyq.q: Describe the salient features of the Watson-Crick model of DNA with a labelled diagram. Name the bonds that (i) link the nucleotides in a strand and (ii) hold the two strands together.
pyq.answer:
The Watson-Crick model describes the secondary structure of B-DNA as a double helix with the following features:

  1. DNA is made of two polynucleotide chains, each a chain of deoxyribonucleotides with a backbone of alternating 2'-deoxyribose sugar and phosphate.
  2. The two chains are antiparallel: one runs 5'→3', the other 3'→5'.
  3. The sugar-phosphate backbones are on the outside and the nitrogen bases project inwards, roughly perpendicular to the axis.
  4. The bases of the two chains are paired by hydrogen bonds: adenine with thymine (two hydrogen bonds) and guanine with cytosine (three hydrogen bonds). A purine always pairs with a pyrimidine, so the two chains are complementary and the helix has a uniform width.
  5. The two chains are coiled around a common axis into a right-handed double helix.
  6. The helix has a pitch of 34 Å (3.4 nm), with 10 base pairs in each turn, so adjacent base pairs are 3.4 Å (0.34 nm) apart.
  7. The stacked base pairs and the hydrogen bonds together stabilise the helix. Other forms of DNA (A, C, Z) also occur.

(i) Within a strand the nucleotides are linked by 3'–5' phosphodiester bonds (covalent). (ii) The two strands are held together by hydrogen bonds between complementary bases (and stabilised by base stacking). Draw the labelled double helix: backbone, base pairs with 2 and 3 dotted lines, 5' and 3' ends, pitch 34 Å, rise 3.4 Å, major and minor grooves. (Features 4 marks, diagram and bonds 1 mark.)

pyq.q:
A student took a piece of fresh liver, ground it in trichloroacetic acid with a mortar and pestle and strained the thick slurry through cheesecloth. She collected the filtrate in a beaker and kept the residue on the cloth. She then took a second weighed piece of liver, dried it in an oven, weighed it again and burnt it fully in a crucible until only a grey powder remained.
(i) Name the two fractions obtained by filtering, and state the range of molecular weights of the compounds in each.
(ii) Name the four types of organic compounds present in the residue on the cloth.
(iii) One of these four types is not a macromolecule. Name it and explain why it is found in the residue.
(iv) What does the grey powder contain and what is it called?
pyq.answer:
(i) The filtrate is the acid-soluble pool, containing micromolecules of molecular weight 18 to about 800 Da; the residue is the acid-insoluble fraction, containing macromolecules of molecular weight 10,000 Da and above. (1 mark)

(ii) Proteins, nucleic acids, polysaccharides and lipids. (1 mark)

(iii) Lipids; their molecular weight is below 800 Da, but in the cell they are arranged in membranes, and on grinding the membranes break into vesicles that are not water-soluble, so they are retained with the macromolecules. (1 mark)

(iv) The grey powder is the ash: all carbon compounds have been oxidised to CO2 and water vapour, and the ash contains the inorganic elements (calcium, magnesium, etc.) and inorganic compounds (sulphate, phosphate). The loss of weight on drying gave the water content. (1 mark)

pyq.q:
In a laboratory experiment, a fixed amount of the enzyme amylase was added to a series of test tubes containing increasing concentrations of starch, all kept at 37 °C and pH 7. The rate of formation of maltose rose steeply at first, then more slowly, and beyond a certain starch concentration did not rise at all. In a second experiment the same tubes were kept at 15 °C, 37 °C, 60 °C and 90 °C: the rate was low at 15 °C, highest at 37 °C, lower at 60 °C and zero at 90 °C. When the 15 °C tube was warmed to 37 °C the rate recovered; when the 90 °C tube was cooled to 37 °C it did not.
(i) Name the maximum rate reached in the first experiment and explain why it is not exceeded.
(ii) To which class of enzymes does amylase belong, and which bond does it break?
(iii) Why did the 15 °C tube recover while the 90 °C tube did not?
(iv) A student added malonate to one tube expecting to inhibit amylase. Was this a sensible choice? Give a reason.
pyq.answer:
(i) The maximum rate is the maximum velocity, Vmax. It is not exceeded because at high substrate concentration all the enzyme molecules are occupied by substrate; there are no free enzyme molecules left to bind the additional starch. (1 mark)

(ii) Amylase is a hydrolase; it hydrolyses the glycosidic bonds between glucose units of starch, releasing maltose. (1 mark)

(iii) Low temperature only preserves the enzyme in a temporarily inactive state, so warming restores activity. High temperature (90 °C) denatures the enzyme: its tertiary structure and active site are destroyed permanently, so cooling does not restore activity. (1 mark)

(iv) No. Malonate is a competitive inhibitor that works only on succinic dehydrogenase, because it closely resembles that enzyme's substrate succinate. Competitive inhibitors are specific to the enzyme whose substrate they resemble; malonate does not resemble starch and will not compete for the active site of amylase. (1 mark)

practice_mcq.q: The most abundant chemical in a living organism is
practice_mcq.explanation: Water makes up 70 to 90 per cent of the total cellular mass (Table 9.1); protein at 10 to 15 per cent is the most abundant organic compound.

practice_mcq.q: The simplest amino acid, whose R group is a hydrogen atom, is
practice_mcq.explanation: Glycine has R = H; alanine has a methyl group and serine a hydroxymethyl group.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following amino acids has an extra amino group and is therefore basic?
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT's examples are glutamic acid (acidic, extra carboxyl), lysine (basic, extra amino group) and valine (neutral); tyrosine is aromatic.

practice_mcq.q: Arachidonic acid has how many carbon atoms, counting the carboxyl carbon?
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT states arachidonic acid has 20 carbon atoms including the carboxyl carbon; palmitic acid has 16.
Glycerol is a three-carbon compound with three hydroxyl groups, i.e. trihydroxy propane; its three −OH groups are esterified with fatty acids to make a triglyceride.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is a purine?
practice_mcq.explanation: Adenine and guanine are purines with a double ring; cytosine, uracil and thymine are single-ring pyrimidines.
Adenosine is adenine attached to ribose, without phosphate, so it is a nucleoside; adenylic acid (AMP) is the nucleotide.

practice_mcq.q: Which of these is a polymer of fructose?
practice_mcq.explanation: Inulin is a fructose polymer; starch, glycogen and cellulose are all homopolymers of glucose.

practice_mcq.q: The exoskeleton of arthropods is made of the complex polysaccharide
practice_mcq.explanation: Chitin, built of N-acetyl glucosamine units, forms the arthropod exoskeleton; peptidoglycan is the bacterial cell-wall polymer.

practice_mcq.q: In a polysaccharide chain, the reducing end is
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT states that the right end of a polysaccharide is the reducing end and the left end the non-reducing end; branched glycogen has one reducing end and many non-reducing ends.

practice_mcq.q: The most abundant protein in the animal world is
practice_mcq.explanation: Collagen, the intercellular ground substance, is the most abundant animal protein; RuBisCO is the most abundant protein in the whole biosphere.

practice_mcq.q: Only which kind of helix is found in the secondary structure of proteins?
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT states that only right-handed helices are observed in proteins; the α-helix is right-handed.

practice_mcq.q: Adult human haemoglobin, an example of quaternary structure, consists of
options: two α and two β subunits
one α and one β subunit
two α and two γ subunits
practice_mcq.explanation: Adult haemoglobin has four subunits, two identical α chains and two identical β chains; γ chains occur in fetal haemoglobin.

practice_mcq.q: In B-DNA the pitch of the helix and the number of base pairs per turn are
practice_mcq.explanation: The pitch is 34 Å (3.4 nm) with 10 base pairs per turn, giving a rise of 3.4 Å per base pair.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following is not a secondary metabolite?
practice_mcq.explanation: Glucose is a primary metabolite with a clear physiological role; morphine (alkaloid), ricin (toxin) and concanavalin A (lectin) are secondary metabolites in Table 9.3.

practice_mcq.q: The essential chemical component of the co-enzymes NAD and NADP is the vitamin
practice_mcq.explanation: NCERT gives NAD and NADP containing niacin as the example of vitamins as components of co-enzymes; riboflavin is in FAD.

practice_mcq.q: Haem is the prosthetic group of
practice_mcq.explanation: In peroxidase and catalase, which break H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub> into water and oxygen, haem is the tightly bound prosthetic group forming part of the active site; zinc is the co-factor of carboxypeptidase.

practice_mcq.q: An enzyme that removes a group from its substrate without hydrolysis, leaving a double bond, belongs to the class
practice_mcq.explanation: Lyases catalyse X−C−C−Y → X−Y + C=C; hydrolases use water, isomerases inter-convert isomers and ligases join two compounds.

practice_mcq.q: Which of the following reactions is not mediated by an enzyme in the body?
options: Dissolving of CO<sub>2</sub> in water to form carbonic acid
Unwinding of the two DNA strands during replication
Formation of a peptide bond on the ribosome
practice_mcq.explanation: This is the exemplar item: CO<sub>2</sub> dissolves in water and forms carbonic acid on its own, slowly (about 200 molecules per hour); carbonic anhydrase only speeds it up. The other three need helicase, sucrase and the ribosome's peptidyl transferase respectively.

common_mistakes: Writing 'all enzymes are proteins'. NCERT says almost all; ribozymes are RNA enzymes. In an Assertion-Reason item this one word decides the answer.

Confusing nucleoside with nucleotide. Nucleoside = base + sugar (adenosine); nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate (adenylic acid). Also confusing which sugar goes where: ribose in RNA, 2'-deoxyribose in DNA; uracil only in RNA, thymine only in DNA.

Calling starch, glycogen or chitin heteropolymers. Cellulose, starch and glycogen are homopolymers of glucose, inulin of fructose, and NCERT calls the complex polysaccharides such as chitin 'mostly homopolymers'. Proteins and gums are the heteropolymers.

Explaining the iodine test the wrong way round or without the reason. Starch turns blue because its helical secondary structure holds iodine; cellulose has no helices and stays colourless. The reason earns the mark, not the colour.

Saying lipids are macromolecules. They are below 800 Da; they appear in the acid-insoluble fraction only because membrane lipids form insoluble vesicles on grinding. State both the fact and the reason.

Giving the wrong reason for the V<sub>max</sub> plateau, such as 'the enzyme gets used up' or 'the product inhibits it'. NCERT's reason is that no free enzyme molecules are left to bind additional substrate; every active site is occupied.

Treating low temperature and high temperature as the same effect. Low temperature keeps the enzyme temporarily inactive and the activity recovers; high temperature denatures it permanently. Examiners look for the word 'temporarily' and the word 'denatured'.
Writing the DNA numbers loosely: pitch 34 Å (not 3.4 Å), 10 base pairs per turn, rise 3.4 Å per base pair. Mixing up the ångström and nanometre values (34 Å = 3.4 nm) loses the fact mark.

Forgetting the examples in the co-factor answer. Haem in catalase and peroxidase (prosthetic group), niacin in NAD and NADP (co-enzyme), zinc in carboxypeptidase (metal ion). Definitions alone rarely get full marks.

Describing the enzyme classes without the reaction type. 'Hydrolases hydrolyse' is not enough; write the bonds (ester, ether, peptide, glycosidic, C−C, C−halide, P−N) and give one enzyme. For lyases, say 'without hydrolysis, leaving a double bond'.
strategy:
Biomolecules is a fact-dense chapter, and the facts are all in NCERT's text, tables and figures. Do not study it from a coaching booklet first; read the NCERT chapter twice, the second time with a pencil, marking every number, name and example. Then prepare it in three sittings.

Sitting 1 (about 1½ hours): the molecules. Learn the analysis method (trichloroacetic acid, acid-soluble pool, acid-insoluble fraction, ash) and Tables 9.1 and 9.2. Draw the amino acid, alanine, the zwitterion, a triglyceride, a nucleoside and a nucleotide from memory. Learn Table 9.3 (secondary metabolites) and Table 9.4 (protein functions) as two-column lists; test yourself by covering one column. Learn the polysaccharide facts: homopolymers, reducing end, the iodine test, chitin.

Sitting 2 (about 1½ hours): the structures. Write the four levels of protein structure in four lines with examples and draw the four-panel diagram. Write the Watson-Crick model as seven numbered points with the three numbers and draw the helix. Illustrate the three bonds of exercise 9.2 on one page. These three pages are your 5-mark answers for structure.

Sitting 3 (about 2 hours): enzymes. This is where the long questions come from. Write the catalytic cycle with its diagram, the activation-energy diagram with the carbonic anhydrase numbers, the three factor graphs with the reasons for each shape, the malonate example, the six classes with one reaction and one enzyme each, and the three co-factors with their examples. Then answer exercise 9.15 (properties of enzymes) as a ten-point list.

Revision: the night before, redo the practice MCQs and the Assertion-Reason items, and redraw the eight diagrams once each. In the paper, give the 5-mark enzyme question a diagram and NCERT phrases ('induces the enzyme to alter its shape', 'no free enzyme molecules'); examiners mark against those phrases.
